The LEANN vector index recomputes embeddings at query time instead of saving them to disk. The repo benchmark shows a 60 million chunk Wikipedia index dropping from 201 GB to 6 GB. The research paper won the Best Research Paper award at MLSys 2026 . So, it brings semantic search and RAG over personal data, on a laptop. TL;DR Size: 6 GB for 60M chunks ( repo ); 4 GB in the paper’s 76 GB Wikipedia setup. Default embedder: Contriever (110M params). It is an index, not an LLM, so no context length applies. Runs on: laptops and workstations. The paper tested an RTX 4090 box with 32 GB RAM and an M1 Ultra Mac. A CPU-only Linux install exists, with no published CPU latency. Performance: matches HNSW downstream accuracy at 90% recall, using under 5% of raw-data storage. Best: 25.5% NQ accuracy, identical to HNSW, using 4 GB instead of 188 GB. Worst: HotpotQA retrieval takes 44.80 s on the Mac, 50.1% of total pipeline time. What is LEANN? LEANN is a low-storage approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index built on top of FAISS . It targets one problem: vector indexes are often bigger than the data they index. The research paper shows a 76 GB corpus needs 173 GB of embeddings plus a 15 GB HNSW graph. That more than doubles the raw data. LEANN keeps a pruned graph, drops the full vectors, and rebuilds them on demand. The code is MIT licensed and installs with uv pip install leann . How does LEANN recompute embeddings without stalling search? Graph indexes like HNSW visit only a small set of nodes per query. LEANN exploits that. It stores the graph plus a compact product quantization (PQ) table. At query time, it re-embeds only nodes on the search path. 3 techniques keep this practical: Two-level search: cheap PQ distances rank neighbors first. Only top candidates get exact recomputation. Dynamic batching: candidates from several hops are grouped, for example 64 at once, for GPU efficiency. High-degree preserving pruning: most nodes keep few edges, while the top 2% “hub” nodes keep more. In ablations, two-level search gives an average 1.4x speedup. Adding batching raises it to 1.8x. Embedding recomputation still accounts for about 76% of query latency. How does LEANN perform on benchmarks? The research team tested NQ, TriviaQA, GPQA and HotpotQA against a 60M-passage RPJ-Wiki datastore. Latency is measured at 90% Recall@3. All figures below are self-reported in the research paper . On NQ, with Qwen3-4B on an RTX 4090, LEANN and HNSW both reach 25.5% downstream accuracy. LEANN uses 4 GB of storage. HNSW uses 188 GB. BM25 scores 18.3%, and PQ compression scores 17.9%. The cost is search time. LEANN retrieval takes 2.48 s on NQ, versus 0.05 s for HNSW. Generation takes about 20 s, so end-to-end latency rises from 20.95 s to 23.34 s. Across datasets on the RTX 4090, LEANN retrieval ranges from 1.12 s (GPQA) to 7.12 s (HotpotQA). The IVF-based recomputation baseline, inspired by EdgeRAG , is up to 200x slower. LEANN improves exact match by up to 11.8% over BM25. The GitHub repo reports similar savings on personal data. 400K chat messages shrink from 1.8 GB to 64 MB. 38K browser entries shrink from 130 MB to 6.4 MB. The post Polymathic AI and Princeton Researchers Release FlashMap, a Flow Map Drafter for 6.14x Faster LLM Decoding appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Researchers from Polymathic AI, Princeton University, USC ISI, NYU and the Flatiron Institute have released FlashMap . FlashMap speculative decoding replaces the discrete diffusion drafter with a continuous flow map. It drafts a full 16-token block in 1 forward pass. Tokens in that block stay consistent with each other. On Qwen3-8B, the research team reports up to 6.14x lossless speedup on GSM8K. Drafter weights for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B are on Hugging Face , with vLLM and SGLang plugins . TL;DR Size: 0.5B-parameter drafter (500M for Qwen3-8B, 475M for Qwen3-4B); drafts blocks of K = 16 tokens. Runs on: the same GPU as the target model. Paper speedups use 1 NVIDIA H200 NVL at concurrency 1, in bf16. Performance: fastest drafter tested on Qwen3-8B, about 7% above a retrained DFlash on average. Best: 6.14x speedup on GSM8K at temperature 0 (acceptance length 7.69 tokens). Worst: 2.28x speedup on Alpaca at temperature 1. On Qwen3-4B (temperature 0), it trails DFlash on 4 of 9 tasks. What is FlashMap? FlashMap is a speculative decoding drafter that maps Gaussian noise to a token block in 1 step. A small drafter proposes K tokens. The target model then checks all K in 1 parallel pass and keeps the longest matching prefix. Output stays exactly what the target would produce. Speed depends on 2 things. How many drafted tokens get accepted, and how cheaply they were drafted. EAGLE-3 drafts autoregressively, so cost grows with block length. DFlash drafts the full block in 1 pass with block diffusion. Why do diffusion drafters lose acceptance? DFlash predicts each slot in the block independently. The research team calls this the factorized approximation. Picture a continuation that is “new york” or “san diego” with equal odds. An independent drafter proposes “new diego” or “san york” half the time. The target rejects those at slot 2. FlashMap builds on Flow Map Language Models . Each noise sample maps to 1 full block. The noise picks the mode for every slot jointly. How does FlashMap work? The drafter is a 6-block diffusion transformer (DiT), with embedding dimension 2048 and 16 attention heads. It reads hidden states from target layers 1, 9, 17, 25 and 33. Embedding matrix and LM head are copied from the target and stay frozen. Training runs in 2 stages: Flow teacher: a continuous flow over one-hot token blocks, trained with cross-entropy. A time reparameterization handles Qwen3’s 151,936-token vocabulary. Flow map student: semigroup distillation turns the flow into a 2-time denoiser. It jumps from noise to data in 1 step. Both drafters train on 500K samples from Open-PerfectBlend . Total compute across all models and ablations was about 4,600 GPU hours on H200s. How does FlashMap compare on benchmarks? The research team retrained EAGLE-3 and DFlash on the same data and settings. Tests cover 9 benchmarks across math, code and chat, at temperatures 0 and 1. Speed: 1-step FlashMap is the fastest drafter on every Qwen3-8B task, at both temperatures. Accuracy: 1-step FlashMap beats DFlash on acceptance length in 15 of 18 settings. It has about half the parameters. Chat gains are largest: at temperature 0, gains over DFlash are 5.5% on math, 11.1% on chat. 2-step mode: acceptance length beats DFlash in 18 of 18 settings, by 10% on average. EAGLE-3: at temperature 1, it has 9% higher acceptance length but runs 35% slower. A shuffle test checks whether drafts use real inter-token structure. At 2 steps, FlashMap recovers most of the joint-structure gain of a 16-step teacher. At 1 step, it keeps only a small fraction. Drafting 4 noise samples as a tree raised speedup by 11% on average. The client, however, is not even thinking of selling the company as they see future growth over the next couple of years that they wish to materialize in order to get a larger exit. The conversation prompted me to consider something I believe many entrepreneurs miss, and it’s this: Revenue can rise while enterprise value falls. When revenue and value move in opposite directions Founders and boards routinely track revenue and profitability over time. But another graph deserves equal attention: enterprise value. Its trajectory can turn downward while the operating numbers continue improving, with significant implications for M&A timing. Consider a hypothetical SaaS company generating $15 million in annual recurring revenue, valued at 6x ARR. Its implied enterprise value is $90 million. Two years later, ARR reaches $20 million, but the multiple falls to 3.5x revenue. Enterprise value drops to $70 million. Revenue increased 33%, while value declined 22%. These are only illustrative assumptions to demonstrate how multiple compression can overshadow operating growth. For a founder postponing a sale until the next revenue milestone, the practical implication is clear: Reaching that milestone may still produce a smaller exit. Qualitative, absolute and relative factors The revenue multiplier reflects several dimensions that evolve differently. Qualitative factors include management quality, founder dependence, competitive intensity, product differentiation and strategic relevance to buyers. Absolute financial measures include revenue, EBITDA and cash flow. Relative performance measures include growth, margins, net revenue retention and gross revenue retention. Although retention metrics are expressed as percentages, their importance lies in what they reveal about customer durability and expansion. Buyers assess these measures together and compare them with relevant peers. As companies mature, their absolute results can improve while their growth rates weaken. Meanwhile, stronger profitability, better retention or deeper management capabilities may support a higher multiplier. The valuation outcome depends on the combined effect. Boards should therefore ask which characteristics will improve over the next year, which could deteriorate and how buyers might price those changes. M&A preparation should begin while you are winning A sale requires preparation, buyer engagement, negotiation and diligence, during which buyers continually reassess performance and forecasts. Waiting until a slowdown becomes visible can weaken negotiating leverage and raise questions about management’s projections. Strategic buyer demand also follows its own timetable. A buyer may place substantial value on acquiring a particular technology, customer base or geographic presence today. That interest can diminish after an internal product launch, a competing acquisition or a budget change. Waiting can still create considerable value when additional scale attracts more buyers, profitability improves or concentration falls. Boards can make that case tangible by reviewing estimated enterprise value alongside the operating plan, using scenarios in which revenue grows while the multiple holds, expands or contracts. They should also consider how debt, cash, dilution, liquidation preferences and transaction terms affect shareholder proceeds. Nobody can reliably identify the valuation peak in advance. However, every decision to delay a sale embeds a view about future valuation. That view deserves its own graph.
